questions.stem: A reducing balance loan with interest rate factor R and a regular repayment d is modelled by:
options: V(n + 1) = R × V(n) − d
V(n + 1) = R × V(n) + d
questions.explanation: Each period interest is added (multiply by R) and then the repayment is subtracted. Adding d instead models an annuity investment, where money is deposited.

questions.stem: An annuity investment, where an initial amount earns compound interest and a regular deposit d is added each period, is modelled by:
options: V(n + 1) = R × V(n) + d
V(n + 1) = R × V(n) − d
questions.explanation: The balance grows by the interest (multiply by R) and by the deposit (add d). Without the + d, the recurrence is a plain compound interest investment.

questions.stem: An interest-only loan is one in which each repayment:
options: pays off an equal share of the principal each period
equals the interest charged, so the balance does not change
repays the principal first, then the interest charged
is less than the interest, so the balance slowly grows
questions.explanation: With interest-only repayments, the interest added each period is exactly cancelled by the repayment, so the principal is still owed in full at the end of the term.

questions.stem: In one row of a loan amortisation table, the reduction in the principal is calculated as:
options: interest − repayment
repayment − interest
repayment + interest
balance − interest
questions.explanation: Part of each repayment covers the interest for the period, and the rest reduces the principal. Subtracting the interest from the balance gives no meaningful quantity.

questions.stem: An annuity is best described as:
options: an investment that provides regular payments that last forever
a loan whose balance stays the same while payments are made
an investment that only grows because regular deposits are made
an investment that provides regular payments until it is used up
questions.explanation: An annuity pays out regular amounts, with interest earned on the remaining balance, until the balance reaches zero. One that lasts forever is the special case called a perpetuity.

questions.stem: Over the life of a reducing balance loan with equal repayments, the interest part of each repayment:
options: decreases
increases
stays the same
is always half
questions.explanation: Interest is charged on the balance, which falls over time, so the interest part shrinks and more of each repayment reduces the principal.

questions.stem: The total interest paid on a reducing balance loan is:
options: the interest rate multiplied by the amount borrowed
the amount borrowed divided by the number of repayments
the first interest charge multiplied by the number of repayments
the total of all repayments minus the amount borrowed
questions.explanation: Everything paid beyond the amount borrowed is interest. Multiplying the first interest charge by the number of repayments overstates it, because the interest falls as the balance falls.

questions.stem: A loan is repaid fortnightly over 20 years. In a finance solver, the number of payments, N, is:
questions.explanation: There are 26 fortnights in a year, so N = 20 × 26 = 520. 240 would be monthly repayments, and 480 assumes two payments each month.

questions.stem: In a finance (TVM) solver, a reducing balance loan that is fully repaid is entered with:
options: PV = 0, PMT negative and FV positive
PV positive, PMT negative and FV = 0
PV negative, PMT positive and FV = 0
PV positive, PMT positive and FV = 0
questions.explanation: From the borrower’s view, the loan amount is money received (positive), each repayment is money paid out (negative), and the balance at the end is zero.

questions.stem: A simple perpetuity can provide regular payments forever because:
options: each payment is less than the interest, so the principal keeps growing
the interest rate on a perpetuity increases as the balance falls
each payment is a fixed share of the principal that will run out
each payment equals the interest earned, so the principal never falls
questions.explanation: In a perpetuity only the interest is withdrawn, so the balance stays the same and the same interest is earned every period. A payment above the interest would make it an annuity that runs out.

questions.stem: Plotted against time, the balance of an annuity paying regular amounts:
options: increases steadily
stays constant
decreases, then increases
decreases to zero
questions.explanation: Each payment is larger than the interest earned, so the balance falls until it is used up. A constant balance would be a perpetuity.

questions.stem: A loan of $180 000 is charged interest at 5.4% per annum, compounding monthly. The interest charged in the first month is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 5.4 ÷ 12 = 0.45%, and 0.45% of 180 000 = $810. $9720 is a full year of interest at 5.4%.

questions.stem: A loan of $240 000 is charged interest at 4.8% per annum, compounding monthly, and repaid at $1500 per month. The balance after the first repayment is:
questions.explanation: Add one month’s interest, 0.4% of 240 000 = $960, then subtract the repayment: 240 000 + 960 − 1500 = $239 460. $238 500 ignores the interest.

questions.stem: A loan of $20 000 is charged interest at 9% per annum, compounding monthly, with repayments of $500 per month. If V(n) is the balance after n months, the recurrence relation is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75%, so R = 1.0075, and the repayment is subtracted. 1.09 applies the annual rate every month.

questions.stem: In a loan amortisation table, the balance is $15 000, the interest rate is 0.5% per month and the repayment is $400. The reduction in the principal for that month is:
questions.explanation: Interest = 0.5% of 15 000 = $75, so the principal falls by 400 − 75 = $325. $75 is the interest part of the repayment, not the principal part.

questions.stem: The sum of $500 000 is invested in a perpetuity at 4.2% per annum, compounding monthly. The monthly payment it provides is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 4.2 ÷ 12 = 0.35%, and 0.35% of 500 000 = $1750. $21 000 is the yearly amount, not the monthly payment.

questions.stem: An investment starts at $10 000, earns 6% per annum compounding monthly, and $200 is added at the end of each month. The balance after 2 months is:
questions.explanation: Month 1: 10 000 × 1.005 + 200 = 10 250. Month 2: 10 250 × 1.005 + 200 = 10 501.25. $10 250 is the balance after one month only.

questions.stem: An annuity of $400 000 earns 5.4% per annum, compounding monthly, and pays $3000 at the end of each month. The balance after the first payment is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 0.45%, so the interest is $1800 and the balance is 400 000 + 1800 − 3000 = $398 800. $397 000 leaves out the interest earned.

questions.stem: An interest-only loan of $420 000 is charged 6% per annum, compounding monthly. The monthly repayment is:
questions.explanation: Interest-only repayments equal the monthly interest: 0.5% of 420 000 = $2100. $25 200 is the interest for a whole year.

questions.stem: A personal loan of $15 000 is repaid with 60 monthly repayments of $311.38. The total interest paid is:
questions.explanation: Total repaid = 60 × 311.38 = $18 682.80, and the interest is 18 682.80 − 15 000 = $3682.80. $18 682.80 is the total cost of the loan, not the interest.

questions.stem: A loan is modelled by V(0) = 25 000, V(n + 1) = 1.006 × V(n) − 600, where n is in months. This describes a loan of $25 000 with:
options: interest at 7.2% p.a. compounding monthly and repayments of $600 per month
interest at 0.6% p.a. compounding monthly and repayments of $600 per month
interest at 6% p.a. compounding monthly and repayments of $600 per month
interest at 7.2% p.a. compounding monthly and deposits of $600 per month
questions.explanation: R = 1.006 means 0.6% per month, which is 12 × 0.6 = 7.2% per annum. The − 600 shows a repayment; a deposit would be added.

questions.stem: An investment is modelled by V(n + 1) = 1.0125 × V(n) + 300, where n is in quarters. The investment earns:
options: 5% p.a. compounding quarterly, with $300 withdrawn each quarter
5% p.a. compounding quarterly, with $300 added each quarter
1.25% p.a. compounding quarterly, with $300 added each quarter
12.5% p.a. compounding quarterly, with $300 added each quarter
questions.explanation: R = 1.0125 is 1.25% per quarter, and 4 × 1.25% = 5% per annum. The + 300 is a deposit, so this is an annuity investment.

questions.stem: An annuity investment has a balance of $52 000. It earns 0.5% interest per month, and $500 is deposited at the end of the month. The new balance is:
questions.explanation: Interest = 0.5% of 52 000 = $260, so the balance becomes 52 000 + 260 + 500 = $52 760. $52 762.50 wrongly earns interest on the deposit made at the end of the month.

questions.stem: One month, a loan balance of $50 000 is charged $250 interest. If interest compounds monthly, the annual interest rate is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 250 ÷ 50 000 = 0.5%, so the nominal annual rate is 12 × 0.5% = 6%. 0.5% is the rate for one month.

questions.stem: A loan of $10 000 is charged 1% interest per month and repaid at $500 per month. The balance after two repayments is:
questions.explanation: After one month: 10 000 × 1.01 − 500 = 9600. After two: 9600 × 1.01 − 500 = 9196. $9000 ignores interest, and $9600 is the balance after one repayment.

questions.stem: An investment is modelled by V(0) = 200 000, V(n + 1) = 1.004 × V(n) − 800. The balance:
options: falls by $800 each month until it reaches zero
rises by $800 each month, because interest is added
falls each month, more slowly as the balance falls
stays at $200 000, because the payment equals the interest
questions.explanation: The interest each period is 0.4% of 200 000 = $800, exactly the payment, so the balance never changes. This is a perpetuity.

questions.stem: A $400 000 mortgage at 6% per annum, compounding monthly, is repaid over 30 years at $2398.20 per month. The total interest paid is:
questions.explanation: Total repaid = 360 × 2398.20 = $863 352, so interest = 863 352 − 400 000 = $463 352. $720 000 is simple interest at 6% for 30 years, which ignores the falling balance.

questions.stem: Partway through a reducing balance loan, the interest rate rises but the repayment stays the same. Compared with before, the loan will:
options: be repaid sooner, because more interest is charged
take the same time to repay, with less total interest
take longer to repay, with less total interest
take longer to repay and cost more in total interest
questions.explanation: A higher rate means more of each repayment goes to interest and less to principal, so the balance falls more slowly. The loan runs longer and more interest is paid overall.

questions.stem: A borrower makes a one-off extra payment of $10 000 off a reducing balance loan and keeps the same regular repayments. The effect is to:
options: increase the interest charged in later months
leave the total interest paid unchanged
reduce the time to repay and the total interest
reduce the regular repayment, but not the time
questions.explanation: A lower balance attracts less interest, so more of each later repayment reduces the principal and the loan finishes sooner with less total interest.

questions.stem: A perpetuity pays $2400 per month. If the interest rate on the perpetuity halves, the monthly payment it can provide becomes:
questions.explanation: A perpetuity pays exactly the interest, which is the rate times the fixed principal. Halving the rate halves the interest, so the payment becomes $1200.

questions.stem: A retiree wants a perpetuity that pays $2000 per month. Interest is 4.8% per annum, compounding monthly. The amount that must be invested is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 0.4%, and the principal P must satisfy 0.004 × P = 2000, so P = 2000 ÷ 0.004 = $500 000. $41 667 divides by the annual rate, 0.048, instead of the monthly rate.

questions.stem: A perpetuity of $360 000 is to pay $1500 per month, with interest compounding monthly. The annual interest rate needed is:
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is 1500 ÷ 360 000 ≈ 0.4167%, and 12 × 0.4167% = 5% per annum. 0.42% is the monthly rate, not the annual rate.

questions.stem: Before the final repayment of a loan, the balance is $280. Interest is 0.5% per month and the usual repayment is $400. To clear the loan exactly, the final repayment must be:
questions.explanation: One more month’s interest is added first: 280 × 1.005 = $281.40, which is the final payment. Paying the usual $400 would overpay by $118.60.

questions.stem: A loan is modelled by V(0) = 20 000, V(n + 1) = 1.01 × V(n) − 150. Which statement is true?
options: The balance stays at $20 000, because the payment equals the interest.
The balance increases, because the $150 payment is less than the $200 interest.
The balance falls by $150 each month, because interest is not charged.
The balance falls by $50 each month, because $200 interest is less than $150.
questions.explanation: The first month’s interest is 1% of 20 000 = $200, and paying only $150 leaves the balance $50 higher. The balance keeps rising, so the loan is never repaid.

questions.stem: Plotted against time, the balance of a reducing balance loan with equal repayments:
options: rises at first, then falls quickly towards the end
falls slowly at first, then more quickly towards the end
falls quickly at first, then more slowly towards the end
falls by the same amount after every single repayment
questions.explanation: Early on, most of each repayment covers interest, so the principal falls slowly; later, less interest leaves more to reduce the principal. The points lie on a curve that steepens.

questions.stem: An investment of $60 000 earns 0.4% interest per month, with $1000 added at the end of each month. Correct to the nearest cent, the balance after 3 months is:
A $300 000 loan at 6% per annum, compounding monthly, costs $1932.90 per month over 25 years or $2149.29 per month over 20 years. Choosing 20 years saves interest of about:
questions.explanation: Total interest is 300 × 1932.90 − 300 000 = $279 870 over 25 years and 240 × 2149.29 − 300 000 = $215 829.60 over 20 years, a saving of about $64 040. $216 is only the difference in monthly repayment.

questions.stem: An annuity of $600 000 earns 3.6% per annum, compounding monthly, and pays $1800 per month. The annuity will:
options: last indefinitely, because $1800 equals the monthly interest
run out after about 27.8 years, because 600 000 ÷ 21 600 ≈ 27.8
run out sooner than 27.8 years, because interest is charged
grow each month, because the interest exceeds the payment
questions.explanation: The monthly interest is 0.3% of 600 000 = $1800, the same as the payment, so the balance never falls and it acts as a perpetuity. Dividing the balance by the yearly payments ignores the interest earned.

questions.stem: A loan balance is $250 000 when the interest rate rises from 6% to 7.2% per annum, compounding monthly. The interest charged in the next month increases by:
questions.explanation: At 6% the monthly interest is 0.5% of 250 000 = $1250; at 7.2% it is 0.6% = $1500. The increase is $250. $3000 is the yearly increase, 1.2% of the balance.

questions.stem: An investment with regular monthly deposits and a reducing balance loan both earn or charge 0.5% per month. A recurrence V(n + 1) = R × V(n) + d with R = 1.005 and d = −800 must describe:
options: the loan, because $800 is subtracted each month
the investment, because R is greater than 1
the investment, because $800 is added each month
either one, because R is the same for both
questions.explanation: Both models have R = 1.005, so R cannot tell them apart; the sign of d does. A subtracted regular amount is a repayment, while an investment with regular deposits adds them.

questions.stem: A row of an amortisation table for an annuity shows: balance $80 000, payment $1200, interest $400. The new balance is:
questions.explanation: The interest earned is added and the payment withdrawn: 80 000 + 400 − 1200 = $79 200. $80 800 subtracts the interest and adds the payment, the reverse of what happens.
